excerpt: Solugen is a Houston company that makes chemicals from biomass and other domestic feedstocks in its Bioforge plants, for energy, water treatment and defence uses. Founded in 2016; won a conditional $213.6M DOE loan guarantee in 2024.
content:
Solugen is an industrial chemicals company based in Houston, Texas. Its Bioforge technology turns biomass into high-demand chemicals that were previously made from fossil fuels, in plants it calls Forges. Its first plant, Bioforge Houston, has been operating since 2021, according to InnovationMap. Solugen's website now describes the company as turning American feedstocks into critical materials for energy systems and national security, and lists four Forge types: Bioforge for organic acids used across oilfield operations, water treatment and corrosion protection; Terraforge for amines and aldehydes; Nitroforge for nitramine energetics used in well completions and mining; and Acroforge.

Solugen's company page says it was founded in 2016 by Gaurab Chakrabarti, a physician-scientist who is CEO, and Sean Hunt, the CTO, who holds a PhD in chemical engineering from MIT.

In June 2024 Solugen received a conditional commitment for a $213.6 million loan guarantee from the US Department of Energy's Loan Programs Office, Chemical Engineering magazine reported. The money is for Bioforge Marshall, a 500,000-square-foot plant in southwest Minnesota that broke ground in April 2024 and is a scaled-up version of the Houston plant. It is meant to make bio-based chemicals for wastewater treatment, construction, agriculture and energy, and Solugen said it expects the plant to cut annual carbon emissions by up to 18 million kilograms. The commitment was conditional on further technical, legal, environmental and financial conditions; we have not found confirmation that the loan has closed.

Solugen sells to industrial and government customers rather than consumers, and it does not publish prices. This profile draws on Solugen's own site and published reporting. Nothing here is paid placement.

pros: Makes chemicals from biomass and domestic feedstocks
Several Forge types serving energy, water and defence markets
Backed by a conditional DOE loan guarantee for its Minnesota plant
cons: DOE loan guarantee was conditional when announced

alternatives.intro: Other companies making bio-based or lower-carbon chemicals. We have not compared products.

items.difference: Uses industrial off-gases rather than plant sugars.

items.difference: Starts from captured CO2 and electricity.
